children: 1913 ET - Japanese stocks are higher, led by chip-related stocks, despite continued uncertainty over the U.S. and Japanese monetary policies. Kioxia Holdings is up 5.6% and Advantest is 4.9% higher. The dollar is at 159.84 yen, compared with Y159.76 as of Thursday's Tokyo stock market close. Investors are closely watching domestic earnings and crude oil prices. Asahi Group Holdings and Asics are scheduled to announce their quarterly results later Friday. The Nikkei Stock Average is up 1.1% at 61494.24. (kosaku.narioka@wsj.com; @kosakunarioka)

1847 ET - Japanese stocks may remain rangebound as uncertainty over the U.S. and Japanese monetary policies continues. Nikkei futures are up 1.1% at 61490 on the SGX. The dollar is at 159.86 yen, compared with Y159.76 as of Thursday's Tokyo stock market close. Investors are focusing on domestic earnings and crude oil prices. Asahi Group Holdings and Asics are set to announce their quarterly results later on Friday. The Nikkei Stock Average fell 0.7% to 60819.36 on Thursday. (kosaku.narioka@wsj.com)

1420 ET - Existing home sales suffered a historic setback in October, Realtor.com says. Existing-home sales plunged to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million, down 5.5% from September's downwardly revised pace of 3.97 million, and 8.8% from a year ago, according to the latest data from the National Association of Realtors. It was the lowest market pace since August 2010. Realtor.com Chief Economist Danielle Hale thinks home sales are likely to remain relatively low for the rest of 2026 as mortgage rates remain high, yet she does not believe it's the new normal, according to a press release. "Instead, it reflects a perfect storm of an abrupt shift in the financial environment and large uncertainties in the pre-election period for both policy and the economy just as the housing market usually slows for the season," she says.(chris.wack@wsj.com)

1329 ET - Travel to the U.S. by Canadian residents continues to recover. Preliminary data indicate Canadian resident return trips from the neighboring country were up 3% on-year in October to 1.9 million, Statistics Canada says. That marks a seventh straight month of annual growth, and includes a 2.2% increase in trips by automobile and 5.6% rise in air travel. Still, travel remains 29% below October 2024 for automobiles and 19.6% down for air travel. U.S.-resident trips to Canada were up 8.1% overall in October to hit 1.5 million, a ninth straight rise. This includes an 8.7% increase in trips by automobile, and 6.5% rise in air travel by Americans. (robb.stewart@wsj.com; @RobbMStewart)

1325 ET - U.S. home-sale prices fell for the fourth week in a row, according to Redfin. The median home-sale price was $388,613, down 0.9% year-over-year. That's four straight weeks of declines after three years of increases, handing homebuyers a bit of relief on top of what they're getting from dipping rates. Monthly housing payments dropped to a 6-week low. The median monthly mortgage payment was $2,755 at a 7.18% mortgage rate, the weekly average. Payments are down from $2,820 a month earlier. Homebuying activity held steady. Pending home sales were essentially flat from a week earlier, though they remain at the lowest level in records dating back to 2021. Dipping mortgage rates likely held off a bigger decline in pending sales. (chris.wack@wsj.com)

1300 ET - Just three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas were seller's markets in October, Rocket says. All three seller's markets are in the Northeast. Nassau County, N.Y., was the number-one seller's market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers. The other seller's markets were Newark, N.J., and Montgomery County, PA. All three seller's markets became less strong seller's markets in October. In Nassau County, there were 28.3% fewer sellers than buyers in September, a bigger gap than October's 24.7%. Newark's gap shrunk from 17.6% to 14.3%, and Montgomery County's shrunk from 20.1% to 12.1%. Milwaukee, which was a seller's market in September, is now balanced, meaning it doesn't favor sellers or buyers. The seller's markets are places where limited homebuilding has kept housing supply tight. (chris.wack@wsj.com)

1226 ET - Hitting the Canadian government's goal of 100 million tons of liquefied natural gas annually by 2050 would stimulate nearly C$1 trillion total investment, support close to a quarter million jobs a year, and contribute C$88 billion to GDP to 2050, a study by S&P Global suggests. It sees a pathway for Canada to become the third largest LNG exporter, but argues the window of opportunity is limited. S&P estimates that reaching the target requires a 2.5-times increase in upstream and critical infrastructure investment and a tripling of upstream drilling activity, all at a time when global development competition is high and there is uncertainty over Canada's permitting, policy stability and associated infrastructure constraints. (robb.stewart@wsj.com; @RobbMStewart)

1217 ET - Inflation looks like it's been going in the wrong direction, Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee says at Yahoo Finance's annual conference. Prices have been rising in "disturbingly persistent categories," he says, including services, healthcare and other sources untied to supply shocks like tariffs or oil prices. That stokes concerns that inflation is coming less from those supply shocks and more from overheating demand, Goolsbee says. "We'd do well to try to prevent it from getting worse," he says. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

1109 ET - Nebius Group's Chief Executive Arkady Volozh is working to tamp down recent concerns among investors over financing the AI buildout. Demand for AI is "real and substantial," he says during the company's quarterly earnings call. "Everything else, like building the capacity and financing it, is just the task. Tasks can be hard, but they all can be solved." Volozh says Nebius's customers are committing for longer and at higher prices, and paying more upfront, and the company expects to have access to financing on attractive terms next year. Nebius also has a strong balance sheet and potential external financing, he says. "The prospects for our business have never been better. Our confidence in what we're building has not changed," he says. (kelly.cloonan@wsj.com)

1026 ET - The rise of artificial intelligence could bring about serious short-term disruptions in the labor market, Fed governor Michael Barr says at an event at Yale University. The extent of that disruption, should AI prove capable of displacing humans, would depend on society's reaction, he says. It would need to invest in new job creation and worker training, connecting workers to new jobs and otherwise mitigating adverse effects for the long term, Barr says. "Now is the time for society to begin to consider how to address these potential challenges - while AI adoption is in its relatively early stages," he says. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

1009 ET - Government bonds offer attractive yields and have favorable valuations making them potential hedges against AI-related risk, PIMCO's Rupert Harrison says in a note. AI stocks are under pressure following the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The sector has also faced increased volatility due to concerns about possible tougher regulations after Democrats victory in the U.S. midterm elections. While U.K. government bonds are likely to offer some hedging against AI risk, a more globally diversified bond portfolio could provide more reliable protection, Harrison says. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0949 ET - Bitcoin falls to a 12-week low as oil prices rise after President Trump damped the prospect of a resolution to the Iran war. Trump said on his Truth Social platform that the U.S. doesn't need a deal with Iran. The comments add further pressure on risk-sensitive bitcoin, which was already hit by jitters around AI trade and index provider MSCI announcing it was removing bitcoin treasury firm Strategy from its benchmarks. Meanwhile, chipmaker Nvidia announced its Chief Executive Jensen Huang was resigning, although this was largely priced in. Bitcoin slides 3% to $71,704, the lowest level since August, LSEG data show. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)
